claims.text: The baseline refractory high-entropy alloy has a complex, multiphase microstructure.
The baseline alloy contains inherent lattice distortions.
Ta is an example of an HCP-promoting or HCP-favoring alloying element.
Increasing the fraction of HCP-inducing elements enhances local lattice distortion.
Increasing the fraction of HCP-inducing elements alters phase stability.
The resulting lattice distortion and phase-stability changes modify dislocation-core structure.
Enhanced local lattice distortion amplifies anharmonic lattice vibrations.
Enhanced lattice distortion and anharmonic vibrations lower the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Lower barriers for dislocation motion make dislocation movement easier at high temperature.
Increasing HCP-inducing-element content lowers Young's modulus at high temperature relative to the baseline.
Increasing HCP-inducing-element content lowers yield strength at high temperature relative to the baseline.
The predicted decreases in modulus and yield strength will be statistically significant.
Thermoelastic phenomena and dislocation mechanics dominate the mechanical response between 800°C and 1200°C.
Secondary-phase formation, nonlinear composition responses, and microstructural heterogeneity may affect the magnitude of softening and modulus reduction.
Alloy variants should be prepared with systematically varied selected-element concentrations while maintaining identical processing protocols.
Failure to observe a consistent, statistically significant decrease in both elastic modulus and yield strength, or observation of a reversed trend, would falsify the proposed directional mechanism.
